archetype.name: Bottom-Feeder (unlucky, but earned)
archetype.definition: A team whose 1-8 record overstates how bad it is by a few wins, but whose league-worst offense and protection problems make it a real bottom-tier team rather than a contender in disguise.

report.headline: A broken offense, not bad luck alone, sank Harbaugh's 1-8 season.
report.take:
This is the same Harbaugh program that won 11 games in each of the last two seasons, but those teams were carried by defense and close-game finishing. In 2024 the defense allowed the fewest points in the league. In 2025 it ranked 6th in EPA allowed and the team won 75% of its one-score games, 3rd in the league, on only a 1.6-point-per-game differential. The offense was already 23rd in EPA last year. That was a fragile formula, and this season every piece of it has failed at once: the offense has fallen to dead last in EPA, the defense has slid to the middle, and the close games have gone the other way.

The engine of the collapse is the line. The Chargers rank 31st in sack rate at 0.105 and have taken 33 sacks over nine games, including eight against Houston. They commit a league-worst 4.9 line penalties a game, and their run EPA of -0.267 is the worst in football. The plan doesn't fit the personnel. Harbaugh runs more than anyone relative to the situation, with a pass rate over expected of -10.2, last in the league, yet the run game ranks 24th in stuff rate and 23rd in yards before contact. Those carries don't set anything up. They leave Herbert in long-yardage passing downs behind a line that can't hold up, and the result has been 19 turnovers.

The points allowed overstate the defense's problems. At 27.4 a game, the scoring defense ranks 28th, but it is 15th in EPA allowed, 7th on third down and 9th in takeaways. Much of that scoring damage comes from an offense that keeps handing over the ball and short fields. The real defensive flaws are narrower: a pass rush that ranks 24th in pressure rate and 30th in sacks, and deep coverage that ranks 30th in EPA. Luck has also piled on. Wins over expected sit at -3.25, last in the league, and the point differential implies 4.3 wins rather than one. Still, a -95 differential is earned, not bad luck.

The Baltimore win shows the formula that still works: no turnovers, 160 rushing yards, and a defense that held the Ravens to 16 on the ground. That is a narrow way to win, especially with only 129 passing yards. The remaining schedule has soft spots (the Jets, Patriots, Raiders and Dolphins), so a few more wins are realistic. A season that started 0-8 is over in every way that matters. What's left to judge is whether the protection and the run-first plan get fixed before 2027.

strengths.title: Defense holds up drive by drive
strengths.body: By efficiency this is a league-average defense: 15th in EPA allowed, 7th in third-down rate and 9th in takeaways. It gets off the field more often than its 27.4 points allowed suggests, because the offense's giveaways keep putting it back on short fields. This is the part of the team most likely to hold steady, since it doesn't depend on the line or the turnover luck.

strengths.title: Sound underneath, sure tackling
strengths.body: The short passing game rarely beats this defense, which ranks 10th in EPA on short throws. Opposing WR1s have scored well under their usual output. It also tackles well, 9th in missed-tackle rate, so short catches don't turn into long gains. That structure should hold, though it depends on the secondary staying healthy.

concerns.title: Protection and discipline up front
concerns.body: The line ranks 31st in sack rate and last in line penalties per game. The low point was eight sacks against Houston. This is a genuine personnel and execution flaw, not a side effect of scheme, and with Pipkins and guard Branson Taylor on injured reserve the depth to fix it isn't there. Herbert has also been taking hits on 19.8% of dropbacks, 31st, and that wears on a quarterback over a season.

concerns.title: Run-first plan with no run game
concerns.body: No team leans further toward the run than the Chargers, and no team gets less from it per play. Run EPA is last in the league, and a stuff rate ranked 24th means early downs keep ending behind the sticks. The plan protects a weak pass-blocking line in theory, but in practice it hands Herbert third-and-long against pressure. Expect it to keep failing unless the play-calling changes.

concerns.title: Giveaways are inflating the points allowed
concerns.body: The offense has 19 turnovers and a turnover differential that ranks 29th. Combined with a defense that ranks 30th in deep-pass EPA, that explains much of the gap between the defense's middling efficiency and its 28th-ranked scoring. Turnovers are partly noisy and should ease somewhat. The sacks and pressure that cause many of them are not noise.

trend.note: The passing EPA bottomed out at Kansas City and the Rams. The last two games were the least damaging of the season through the air, and the Baltimore win came with zero turnovers. One clean game after eight losses is a flicker, not a turn yet.

nextGame.headline: Jets' leaky short-pass defense invites Herbert to throw first.
nextGame.body:
The Chargers are 3-point home favorites indoors against a 2-8 Jets team that is mediocre rather than terrible, 23rd in net EPA. The matchup asks the Chargers to change their habits. The Jets stop the run well, 10th in rush EPA allowed, but their pass defense is 30th in EPA and 31st on short throws, with a success rate allowed that ranks 29th. They have also been soft against tight ends and second receivers. That points toward Gadsden, Kolar and Quentin Johnston on quick throws, the kind of passing that also keeps the ball out of the hands of a pass rush that ranks 12th in sacks. Tre Harris draws the toughest assignment: the Jets have held WR1s well under their usual output. On the other side, the Jets' line gives up sacks at a 26th-ranked rate and converts short yardage poorly. That gives a modest Chargers pass rush a rare favorable matchup.

Availability is unsettled on both sides. Ladd McConkey (back) and DT Justin Eboigbe (ankle) sat out against Baltimore, with return estimates pointing to this game. Tackle Trey Pipkins was not activated from injured reserve, and guard Branson Taylor is on IR into December, so the thin line stays thin. For the Jets, Geno Smith, who has started every game, is questionable with an ankle injury after tests found nothing major. Guard Dylan Parham and receiver Omar Cooper Jr. are also questionable, while corner Jarvis Brownlee Jr. is out. Losing Brownlee weakens a secondary that is already the Jets' soft spot.

waysToWin.title: Quick game to tight ends and WR2
waysToWin.body: The Jets rank 31st in short-pass EPA allowed and leak production to tight ends and second receivers. Short, rhythm throws attack that weakness and limit the time Herbert spends behind a struggling line. This only works if Harbaugh is willing to throw on early downs.

waysToWin.title: Repeat the clean Baltimore game
waysToWin.body: The Jets rank 20th in takeaways and don't produce many turnovers on their own. If the Chargers play another zero-turnover game, their middling defense rarely has to defend short fields, and a low total of 40.5 suits a grinding script.

waysToWin.title: Win third down against a shaky line
waysToWin.body: The Chargers' third-down defense ranks 7th, while the Jets give up sacks often and rank 31st in short-yardage conversion. Stalling Jets drives is realistic, especially if Smith is limited by the ankle.

waysToLose.title: Running into the Jets' strength
waysToLose.body: If the Chargers keep their league-low pass rate, they are feeding the worst run game in football into a top-10 run defense. That creates the third-and-long situations where sacks and interceptions have followed all season.

waysToLose.title: Protection breaks down again
waysToLose.body: The Jets' sack total ranks 12th, and the Chargers' patched line ranks 31st in sack rate. A Houston-style afternoon of drive-killing sacks would erase whatever the matchup offers through the air.

waysToLose.title: Getting beaten over the top
waysToLose.body: The Chargers rank 30th in deep-pass EPA allowed, and the Jets' offense is 10th in success rate. A healthy Smith hitting one or two shots could decide a low-scoring game.

nextGame.watch: How often the Chargers throw on first down in the first half. If they still lean on the run against the Jets' strength, the edge in this matchup goes unused.

restOfSeason.body:
Some regression in the Chargers' favor is coming. Wins over expected at -3.25 and a winless record in one-score games before Baltimore are about as unlucky as it gets, and a defense that is average by EPA should allow fewer points once the turnovers ease. The schedule cooperates in spots. The Jets, Patriots, Raiders and Dolphins all rank 24th or worse in defensive EPA except the Jets, who rank 24th exactly. The losing in the remaining games will come against San Francisco and the two division leaders.

What won't regress is the offense's core problem. Pass protection, line penalties and a run game with no push are structural, and the injured reserve list on the line makes a midseason fix unlikely. A realistic finish is a few more wins built on clean, low-scoring games. The offense is likely to stay near the bottom of the league, and the season ends with no playoff relevance and a long offseason around the offensive line.
swingFactors: Turnover count, the biggest driver of the points allowed
Whether Harbaugh shifts toward the short passing game
Offensive line health with Pipkins and Taylor on IR

confidence.note: Nine games of consistent offensive failure make the profile clear. Close-game luck and turnover swings make the win total noisy.
